paragraphs: Finding equilibrium strategies in games with hidden information becomes difficult when the game is too large to examine comprehensively. Counterfactual Regret Minimization, or CFR, is a common approach, but many improvements to its convergence speed do not work under Monte Carlo sampling. That restricts their usefulness for training in large games.

The paper introduces MCCFVFP, a Monte Carlo algorithm that combines counterfactual value calculations from CFR with the best-response strategy of fictitious play. The combination uses these value estimates within a different strategy-improvement approach. The authors identify games containing a high proportion of dominated strategies as a setting where fictitious play offers particular advantages.

In experiments involving poker and other test games, MCCFVFP converged approximately 20%–50% faster than the advanced Monte Carlo CFR variants used for comparison. This is an empirical improvement in the tested games, rather than a universal speed guarantee. The contribution is a way to accelerate equilibrium learning while retaining the sampling-based operation needed for larger games.
neurips-2024-accelerating-nash-equilibri.tldr: MCCFVFP combines counterfactual values with fictitious play and converges approximately 20%–50% faster than advanced Monte Carlo CFR variants in tested games.

paragraphs: Evidential deep learning asks one neural network to learn a distribution over its predictive distribution, with the aim of representing uncertainty. This paper examines whether useful downstream performance actually demonstrates reliable uncertainty estimates. Earlier analyses raised a specific concern: the uncertainty attributed to limited knowledge can remain even when unlimited data is available.

The authors unify several training objectives to sharpen the analysis of how a broad class of these methods behaves as data grows. They also offer a different interpretation: the methods can be understood as energy-based approaches to detecting inputs outside the training distribution. Extensive ablation studies on real-world datasets examine their empirical behavior alongside this theoretical analysis.

The conclusion separates practical effectiveness from faithful uncertainty measurement. In the authors' analysis, downstream successes can occur despite poor uncertainty quantification. Their investigation suggests that incorporating model uncertainty can improve both the faithfulness of uncertainty estimates and performance on representative tasks. That proposed improvement comes with additional computational complexity, making the tradeoff explicit.
neurips-2024-are-uncertainty-quantificat.tldr: The paper argues that evidential deep learning can succeed on downstream tasks despite unreliable uncertainty estimates, and suggests a more computationally costly remedy.

paragraphs: Models that combine different kinds of components are difficult to analyze theoretically. One example is a graph neural network augmented with persistent homology, which supplies information about topological structure. Although these combinations are increasingly used, understanding how their learned predictions extend beyond training data has remained a gap.

The paper introduces a compositional PAC-Bayes framework: a general recipe for deriving generalization bounds for models with heterogeneous layers or submodels. It provides what the authors identify as the first data-dependent bounds for a widely used family of persistent-homology vectorizations, including persistence landscapes, images, and silhouettes, and for graph networks incorporating these features. The framework also yields bounds for ordinary graph and neural networks.

These bounds serve a design purpose as well as an analytical one. The authors use them to construct regularizers that guide model training. Across several standard real-world datasets, the bounds strongly correlate with observed generalization, and the resulting regularizers improve classifier design. The findings connect theoretical analysis of mixed architectures to practical choices about how to train them.
neurips-2024-compositional-pac-bayes-gen.tldr: A compositional PAC-Bayes framework gives generalization bounds for heterogeneous models and uses them to design useful regularizers.

paragraphs: The paper studies how websites communicate permission and restrictions around data used to train general-purpose AI. It audits 14,000 domains underlying major web corpora, tracking changes over time. The focus is on codified preferences, including Terms of Service and robots.txt, and whether these mechanisms provide consistent signals about acceptable use.

The audit finds growing use of AI-specific restrictions, differences in how AI developers are treated, and disagreements between websites' terms and crawling instructions. During 2023–2024, the authors report that sources accounting for roughly 5% or more of C4's tokens became fully restricted, alongside 28% or more of its actively maintained critical sources. They separately report Terms of Service crawling restrictions covering 45% of C4.

The authors interpret these findings as evidence that existing web protocols are poorly suited to widespread reuse for AI. If respected or enforced, the restrictions affect the diversity, freshness, and scaling of available training data. The concern extends to academic and noncommercial research, while also exposing difficulties creators face in expressing meaningful data-use preferences.
neurips-2024-consent-in-crisis-the-rapid.tldr: An audit of 14,000 web domains finds rapidly increasing AI data restrictions and inconsistent mechanisms for expressing consent.

paragraphs: Combining camera and radar information can improve 3D object detection, but moving objects complicate the use of observations from different times. Earlier radar-camera methods using a bird's-eye view can struggle to capture this motion effectively. CRT-Fusion addresses the problem by making motion estimation part of the process that combines sensor information over time.

Its first module merges image and radar features in both camera and bird's-eye views to build a unified representation. A second module simultaneously estimates pixel-level velocity and segments the bird's-eye view. A third uses the resulting velocity estimates and occupancy scores to align and recurrently combine feature maps from multiple timestamps. Motion therefore helps determine how earlier observations contribute to the current representation.

On nuScenes, the authors report state-of-the-art results for radar-camera 3D detection, with improvements of +1.7% in NDS and +1.4% in mAP over the respective leading comparisons. These results support the usefulness of motion-guided temporal fusion for producing more accurate and robust detection features in the evaluated setting.
neurips-2024-crt-fusion-camera-radar-tem.tldr: CRT-Fusion uses estimated motion to align camera-radar features across time, improving 3D object detection on nuScenes.

paragraphs: Dynamic Gaussian Splatting methods represent a scene's structure with Gaussian elements and use a neural network to model movement. They support fast rendering and extraction of scene elements, but changing how an object moves over time remains difficult. The paper focuses on making these dynamic representations more directly editable.

An existing approach, Sparse Controlled Gaussian Splatting with deformed control points, partly addresses this need. However, it requires selecting elements to hold fixed and centroids to adjust, and reproducing edits presents further difficulties. D-MiSo introduces a mesh-inspired representation of dynamic Gaussian scenes to provide another basis for controlling changes.

The method links parameterized Gaussian splats into a triangle-soup structure associated with an estimated mesh. This organization allows new trajectories to be constructed separately for the 3D objects within a scene. The stated capability is to edit scene dynamics over time, including edits that preserve part of the existing motion. Its contribution is therefore a representation and linking strategy that connects scene reconstruction to object-level control of movement.
neurips-2024-d-miso-editing-dynamic-3d-s.tldr: D-MiSo links Gaussian splats through a mesh-inspired representation so individual objects' trajectories can be edited while retaining partial dynamics.

paragraphs: Forecasting becomes unreliable when the statistical distribution of a time series changes quickly. Normalization methods try to reduce these changes before a forecasting model processes the data. The paper argues that methods using fixed periods or windows in the time domain can struggle because the underlying temporal patterns are complex.

Dual-domain Dynamic Normalization, or DDN, uses a wavelet transform to separate the series into components at different frequencies. This representation exposes distribution changes associated with periods that vary over time. DDN then applies normalization in both the frequency and time domains using sliding windows, aiming to reduce non-stationarity through both views of the same signal.

The method is designed as a module that can be incorporated into other forecasting models. Experiments on public benchmarks with different forecasting models show advantages over the other normalization methods evaluated. The findings suggest that preprocessing can benefit from accounting for changing frequency structure as well as local time-domain behavior, without requiring an entirely new forecasting architecture.
neurips-2024-ddn-dual-domain-dynamic-nor.tldr: DDN normalizes changing time series in both time and frequency domains, improving forecasting across the tested models and benchmarks.

paragraphs: Deformable image registration aligns medical images despite differences in shape. Classical methods optimize the alignment directly, while learning-based methods learn how to perform it. This paper investigates which properties of the data, available supervision, and distribution changes help explain when either approach performs well.

The authors find a strong correspondence between classical registration performance and the mutual information between pixel intensities and labels. This suggests that changing a learned model's architecture is unlikely to remove the underlying relationship or its effect on performance. They examine that hypothesis using state-of-the-art classical and learning-based methods, grounding the comparison in the information available in the images.

Weak supervision gives learning-based methods an additional capability: high-fidelity alignment of both intensities and labels that classical methods cannot achieve in the studied comparison. However, the learned features do not make these methods invariant to domain shift; performance remains sensitive to changes in the data distribution. The paper therefore reassesses expectations around label supervision, training time, and generalization under even minor distribution shifts.
neurips-2024-deep-learning-in-medical-im.tldr: The paper connects registration performance to intensity-label information and finds that weak supervision helps learned methods without ensuring robustness to domain shifts.

paragraphs: The paper addresses channel simulation, focusing on schemes that can be implemented practically. Its central concern is what happens when many uses of a channel must be simulated together. The authors identify a scaling problem in existing methods: they do not handle increasing numbers of simultaneous channel uses well enough to benefit from processing them jointly.

Joint simulation offers amortization gains, meaning that the cost can be shared across many channel uses. The proposed direction draws on error-correcting code theory to make this larger-scale operation feasible. Scalability is therefore part of the route to improved performance, because it enables the algorithm to exploit gains that become available when channel uses are grouped.

As a concrete example, the paper shows how polar codes can efficiently simulate independent, identically distributed copies of a class of binary-output channels. The example has a specific scope: the stated construction concerns that channel class and repeated independent uses. It illustrates how coding techniques can support practical channel simulation that benefits from operating at larger scale.
neurips-2024-fast-channel-simulation-via.tldr: The paper uses error-correcting code techniques to scale channel simulation, demonstrating polar-code constructions for a class of binary-output channels.

paragraphs: Sliced Wasserstein methods compare probability distributions through simpler sliced representations and are attractive for their computational and statistical scalability. However, their usual formulations assume a homogeneous domain. The paper addresses joint distributions whose components live on different kinds of domains, where ordinary slicing does not adequately capture the structure of the combined support.

The authors introduce two operators to accommodate this heterogeneity. The Partial Generalized Radon Transform applies nonlinear transformations to a subset of arguments. The Hierarchical Hybrid Radon Transform combines a partial transform with multiple domain-specific versions of that generalized operator. This construction allows different marginal domains to receive transformations suited to their structure within a joint comparison.

Using the hierarchical operator, the paper defines Hierarchical Hybrid Sliced Wasserstein distance, or H2SW. It studies the distance's topological, statistical, and computational properties and reports favorable results in 3D mesh deformation, deep mesh autoencoders, and dataset comparison. The contribution extends scalable distribution comparison to mixed-domain settings where the standard slicing operators are insufficiently expressive.
neurips-2024-hierarchical-hybrid-sliced-.tldr: H2SW extends sliced Wasserstein comparison to heterogeneous joint distributions using hierarchical, domain-specific slicing operators.

paragraphs: Image Textualization addresses a problem with the descriptions used to train image-related AI systems: readily available text often provides an unreliable or incomplete account of an image. Web descriptions can be noisy, while human-written captions are frequently brief. Hiring people to write detailed descriptions is possible, but its cost constrains how much data can be produced.

The proposed framework automatically creates detailed image descriptions by combining existing multimodal large language models with several specialist vision models. Multimodal models work with images and language, while the vision experts contribute visual analysis. The central idea is to make these models collaborate in producing descriptions, offering a way to expand detailed annotation without relying entirely on human labeling.

The authors report experiments supporting the quality of the generated descriptions. They also use the resulting dataset to fine-tune multimodal language models, which then produce substantially longer, more detailed descriptions with fewer hallucinations—claims about content that is not actually present. These findings suggest that the dataset can help models describe more of an image while reducing unsupported additions.
neurips-2024-image-textualization-an-aut.tldr: Image Textualization combines multimodal language models and vision experts to generate detailed image descriptions that improve description richness and reduce hallucinations when used for fine-tuning.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a random walk for drawing uniform samples from high-dimensional convex bodies. The objective is to produce samples whose distribution approaches the uniform target while keeping the computation efficient. The authors report state-of-the-art runtime complexity together with stronger guarantees about the distribution of the output than were previously known.

Those guarantees are expressed in Rényi divergence, a way of measuring the discrepancy between distributions. In the stated result, this control also implies guarantees in total variation, Wasserstein-2 distance, KL divergence, and chi-squared divergence. The significance is that the analysis establishes accuracy in a form that supports several other measures of sampling error.

The proof uses a stochastic diffusion perspective rather than the approaches previously used for polynomial-time algorithms for this problem. It establishes contraction toward the target distribution, with the convergence rate governed by functional isoperimetric constants of the stationary density. The contribution therefore combines an efficient sampling procedure with an analytical approach linking convergence to properties of the target distribution.
neurips-2024-in-and-out-algorithmic-diff.tldr: A new random walk samples convex bodies with state-of-the-art runtime complexity and stronger distributional guarantees proved through a diffusion perspective.

paragraphs: The Monge problem seeks an efficient map from one probability distribution to another, with efficiency determined by a chosen transport cost. This paper studies elastic costs, which add a regularizer to squared Euclidean distance. The extra term shapes how points move, allowing displacement structure to influence which transport map is preferred.

The first contribution is a numerical method for computing provably optimal Monge maps for any elastic cost. This provides a way to construct synthetic problems with known ground-truth transport maps. The second contribution is a loss for learning the parameters of the regularizer, so the structure encouraged by the transport cost can itself be inferred.

The authors apply this learning procedure to a regularizer that encourages displacements within a low-dimensional subspace. On synthetic data generated using their first contribution, they recover that subspace almost perfectly from samples alone. They also report predictive improvements on single-cell data tasks. Together, the two contributions connect controlled tests with a practical method for learning how transport displacements should be structured.
neurips-2024-learning-elastic-costs-to-s.tldr: The paper constructs optimal transport maps for elastic costs and learns regularizers that encourage useful low-dimensional displacement structure.

paragraphs: A useful environmental map should distinguish lasting surroundings from temporary objects. This paper uses repeated camera traversals of the same region to learn that distinction. Its key observation is that the environment stays consistent across traversals while objects frequently change, providing a source of supervision without human annotations.

The proposed 3D Gaussian Mapping framework builds an offline Gaussian-based map from RGB videos while also segmenting temporary objects in 2D. It treats environmental pixels as inliers to a shared 3D representation and object pixels as outliers. Robust feature distillation, feature residual mining, and robust optimization support this joint separation and mapping process.

To evaluate the approach, the authors introduce Mapverse, drawing on Ithaca365 and nuPlan. The evaluation covers unsupervised 2D segmentation, 3D reconstruction, and neural rendering, with results supporting the method's effectiveness and potential for robotics and self-driving. The central dependency is the repeated-traversal signal: consistency across visits helps identify what belongs in the environmental map, while changing content helps reveal temporary objects.
neurips-2024-memorize-what-matters-emerg.tldr: 3D Gaussian Mapping uses repeated camera traversals to jointly learn an environmental map and segment temporary objects without human annotations.

paragraphs: Pooling stereotactic EEG data across people could support larger training datasets, but electrode recordings do not line up neatly between individuals. Each person has a different number of electrodes at locations chosen for clinical needs. The paper introduces seegnificant, a framework designed to learn across this variability rather than require a direct correspondence between recording sites.

The architecture first uses convolutions to turn activity within each electrode into tokens. Attention across time captures longer temporal dependencies. The model then incorporates each electrode's 3D location and applies attention across electrodes to learn spatial and temporal representations. Subject-specific output heads use these representations for decoding tasks.

The authors train a combined model on 21 subjects performing a behavioral task. It predicts each trial's response time using neural data alone. Representations learned through multi-person pretraining also transfer to new subjects with few examples. These findings demonstrate cross-subject decoding and transfer in the evaluated task, supporting the framework as a scalable approach to integrating heterogeneous sEEG recordings.
neurips-2024-neural-decoding-from-stereo.tldr: Seegnificant combines electrode activity and location to decode behavior across subjects and transfer learned representations to new people with few examples.

paragraphs: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning starts with a policy trained on stored data and improves it through new interactions. The transition can be difficult because the evaluation and improvement procedures suitable for offline data do not necessarily match the online environment. The paper targets these mismatches with the aim of supporting more general combinations of offline and online methods.

Before online fine-tuning, the approach reconstructs the pessimistic offline critic through an optimistic reevaluation. It then calibrates this critic using the reliable offline actor, bringing the value estimates into alignment with the existing policy to avoid erroneous updates. Once that preparation is complete, constrained fine-tuning addresses the distribution shift encountered during online learning.

The design separates preparing a useful critic from controlling subsequent policy changes, while addressing both within one procedure. Experiments on multiple simulated tasks show stable and efficient improvement compared with state-of-the-art methods. These results support the approach's practical usefulness in the tested settings; the ambition to connect arbitrary offline and online methods remains a stated design objective rather than a universal empirical guarantee.
neurips-2024-optimistic-critic-reconstru.tldr: The method prepares an optimistic, calibrated critic and constrains online fine-tuning to improve the transition from offline to online reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Tabular datasets vary widely across applications, making it difficult for a single deep-learning approach to work well throughout this diversity. Transformer models that learn from examples supplied in context have shown promise on smaller, simpler tables. This paper addresses their difficulty scaling to larger and more complex datasets.

The proposed approach combines nearest-neighbor retrieval with task-specific fine-tuning. Retrieval gathers a local subset of relevant data, and fine-tuning adapts the transformer with those neighbors in its context. Applied to TabPFN, the resulting method is called LoCalPFN, or locally calibrated PFN. The local examples and model adaptation work together to specialize the base in-context learner.

The authors evaluate LoCalPFN on 95 OpenML datasets curated by TabZilla. They report state-of-the-art performance in this evaluation, including against tuned tree-based models, and a substantial improvement over the base in-context model. The findings show that retrieval and fine-tuning can extend the usefulness of tabular in-context learning to the more demanding datasets studied, rather than relying on the unchanged base model.
neurips-2024-retrieval-fine-tuning-for-i.tldr: LoCalPFN combines nearest-neighbor retrieval and task-specific fine-tuning to improve TabPFN and achieve leading results on 95 evaluated tabular datasets.

paragraphs: Diffusion models generate samples by numerically following a path from a Gaussian reference distribution toward clean data. The choice of steps along this path affects sample quality. This paper tackles how to choose that discretization schedule systematically, rather than depending on handcrafted schedules or manual search.

The authors derive a cost that measures the work performed by the simulation when transporting samples between successive points on the diffusion path. Their algorithm adaptively chooses a schedule that is optimal with respect to this cost. It responds to the path's dynamics and geometry, requires no hyperparameter tuning, and uses only evaluations of the estimated Stein score.

Because it relies on that score, the method can operate with existing pretrained models at inference time or online during training. Experiments show that the learned schedules recover effective choices previously found through manual search and achieve competitive image FID scores. The optimality claim concerns the derived transport-work objective; the sample-quality evidence is the reported competitive empirical performance.
neurips-2024-score-optimal-diffusion-sch.tldr: An adaptive diffusion scheduler minimizes a derived transport-work cost without hyperparameter tuning and achieves competitive image-generation results.

paragraphs: Comparing time-series anomaly detectors is difficult when datasets contain flaws, evaluation measures introduce bias, and methods are tested inconsistently. TSB-AD addresses these problems together. Its purpose is to make conclusions about detector quality rest on curated data, a carefully examined measure, and a common evaluation procedure.

The benchmark includes 1,070 time series drawn from 40 datasets, with curation combining human judgment and model interpretation. The authors examine weaknesses in evaluation measures and identify VUS-PR as the most reliable and accurate measure in their analysis. They evaluate 40 algorithms, ranging from statistical approaches to foundation models, using thorough hyperparameter tuning and a unified setup.

The results challenge the assumption that more advanced neural architectures generally perform best: simpler architectures and statistical methods often do better. At the same time, neural networks show promise for multivariate cases, and foundation models show promise for point anomalies. These distinctions make the benchmark useful for understanding where different approaches succeed, rather than reducing the findings to a single universally superior model family.
neurips-2024-the-elephant-in-the-room-to.tldr: TSB-AD improves anomaly-detection benchmarking and finds that simpler methods often outperform advanced neural architectures, with strengths varying by setting.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can become expensive when an environment has many states or actions. This paper studies whether representations learned in source environments can reduce that dependence when learning in a target environment. It assumes particular latent low-rank structures in the transition kernels of the source and target Markov decision processes.

The analysis covers Tucker ranks (S, d, A), (S, S, d), (d, S, A), and (d, d, d), where S and A describe state and action space sizes. For each setting, the authors introduce a transfer-ability coefficient, alpha, that measures how difficult representation transfer is. Their algorithm learns source representations and exploits the resulting linear structure in the target task.

Depending on the setting, the target regret bound removes dependence on S, A, or their product. Information-theoretic lower bounds also establish minimax optimality with respect to alpha for the algorithms outside the fully low-rank (d, d, d) case. The results specify both benefits of structural transfer and limits on how favorably its difficulty can enter the guarantees.
neurips-2024-the-limits-of-transfer-rein.tldr: Under specified low-rank transition structures, transferred representations reduce target-learning complexity, with matching transfer-difficulty lower bounds in three settings.

paragraphs: The Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, or HSIC, is a kernel-based measure used to study statistical independence. Many estimators already exist, but this paper addresses a more fundamental question: how quickly can any estimator approach the true value as the number of observations grows? Answering this establishes a benchmark for judging existing estimation methods.

The authors prove a minimax optimal estimation rate of order n to the power of minus one-half. The result applies on Euclidean space to classes of Borel probability measures containing Gaussian distributions, using kernels that are continuous, bounded, translation-invariant, and characteristic. These conditions define the scope of the theorem rather than a claim about every possible kernel or distribution class.

Minimax optimality concerns the best achievable worst-case rate over the stated class. The result implies that several frequently used methods, including U-statistic, V-statistic, and Nyström-based estimators, already attain that rate. Its contribution is to establish a fundamental statistical limit and show that familiar estimators meet it under the specified assumptions.
neurips-2024-the-minimax-rate-of-hsic-es.tldr: The paper proves an optimal n⁻¹ᐟ² worst-case rate for HSIC estimation under specified kernel and distribution assumptions, validating several common estimators.

paragraphs: The paper investigates why transformers struggle with arithmetic involving long numbers. The authors suggest that much of the difficulty comes from tracking each digit's exact position within a number. Their intervention adds an embedding to every digit that records its position relative to the beginning of that number.

These embeddings improve performance on their own and also enable further gains from input injection and recurrent layers. With digit positions made explicit, the authors examine logical extrapolation: whether a model can solve arithmetic problems larger and more complex than those encountered during training. This makes the representation of numbers central to the study of generalization.

Training on 20-digit numbers for one day using a single GPU yields up to 99% accuracy on 100-digit addition problems, which the authors report as state-of-the-art performance. They also find improvements in sorting and multiplication. The results demonstrate strong extrapolation in the studied tasks and support the view that resolving digit positions can unlock both arithmetic gains and benefits from architectural changes.
neurips-2024-transformers-can-do-arithme.tldr: Explicit digit-position embeddings help transformers extrapolate from 20-digit training numbers to 100-digit addition, reaching up to 99% accuracy.

paragraphs: Vision-language navigation requires an agent to follow human instructions through a sequence of actions. Training through behavioral cloning or manually engineered rewards can struggle with accumulating errors and matching the expert's overall behavior. This paper proposes learning the joint distribution of navigation states and actions to address that broader alignment problem.

The Energy-based Navigation Policy assigns lower energy to state-action pairs that an expert is more likely to perform. Its training objective combines action likelihood with modeling how navigation states evolve. The authors show that the objective is equivalent to minimizing forward divergence between the expert's occupancy measure and the model's, connecting training to the distribution of state-action visits.

This gives the method an explicit route toward aligning behavior across navigation, rather than evaluating action imitation in isolation. Applied with several navigation architectures, ENP produces promising results on R2R, REVERIE, RxR, and R2R-CE. The evidence supports the usefulness of this policy formulation across the tested architectures and benchmarks, without establishing that accumulated navigation errors are eliminated.
neurips-2024-vision-language-navigation-.tldr: ENP models joint state-action behavior with an energy-based policy to better align instruction-following navigation with expert trajectories.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can recognize the broad subject of an image while missing a small but decisive detail. VisMin tests this finer understanding by asking models to match two closely related images with two closely related captions. Each pair changes only one aspect: an object, an attribute, an object count, or a spatial relationship.

This design emphasizes distinguishing similar images given language, extending the focus of benchmarks centered on distinguishing captions for one image. The authors create examples automatically with language and diffusion models, then use a four-step human verification process. The controlled changes help isolate whether a model understands the specific difference that determines the correct match.

Experiments reveal notable weaknesses in counting and spatial relationships among current models. The authors also generate a larger training dataset and fine-tune CLIP and Idefics2 on it. Both improve substantially on fine-grained understanding across multiple benchmarks, and CLIP additionally improves in general image-text alignment. The work therefore supplies both a targeted evaluation and training data that helps address the measured capabilities.
neurips-2024-vismin-visual-minimal-chang.tldr: VisMin tests minimal visual differences, exposes counting and spatial-reasoning weaknesses, and supplies training data that improves CLIP and Idefics2.

paragraphs: Real-time object detectors must balance accuracy with the time and computation needed to produce predictions. This paper identifies two sources of inefficiency in YOLO models: reliance on non-maximum suppression after prediction and computational redundancy within model components. YOLOv10 addresses both the post-processing stage and the architecture.

The authors introduce consistent dual assignments for training without non-maximum suppression, maintaining competitive detection performance while reducing inference latency. They also optimize components through a design strategy that considers efficiency and accuracy together. The resulting model family is intended for end-to-end detection across several model sizes.

The reported comparisons show substantial gains in the evaluated settings. YOLOv10-S is 1.8 times faster than RT-DETR-R18 at similar average precision on COCO, with 2.8 times fewer parameters and FLOPs. YOLOv10-B has 46% lower latency and 25% fewer parameters than YOLOv9-C at the same performance. These results support the combined value of removing the post-processing dependency and reducing architectural overhead, with the authors reporting state-of-the-art efficiency and performance across model scales.
neurips-2024-yolov10-real-time-end-to-en.tldr: YOLOv10 combines training without non-maximum suppression and architecture optimization to improve the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in real-time object detection.
